findings.reason: The state supplier proves uniqueness of integral-equation solutions. Step 3.1 applies that uniqueness to an arbitrary absolutely continuous solution of the differential equation without establishing its integral equation. The available supplier thm-fundamental-theorem-of-calculus-for-absolutely-continuous-functions requires Countable Choice and Dependent Choice; this lemma assumes only Countable Choice.
findings.remaining_prerequisite: A proof under Countable Choice alone that every admitted absolutely continuous differential solution satisfies the integral equation, or an explicit Dependent Choice hypothesis for uniqueness.
findings.qualification: This identifies an unsupported inference in the present proof, not a refutation of uniqueness under Countable Choice alone.

findings.reason: An exact residual at one returned stage vector does not make the stopped stage procedure equal to the implicit solution map on a neighborhood. Switching to implicit differentiation at that point can return a derivative different from the actual finite NLP derivative.

counterexample.data: One implicit-Euler cell with T=h=1/2, x0=0, f(t,x,u)=x+u, U_c=[-1,1], Omega_x=Omega_u=R, L=0, phi(x)=x, and tau_s>0.
counterexample.calculation: The prescribed seed is K^(0)=u and R(K;u)=K/2-u. For |u|<2 tau_s, Newton returns its initial seed, so the actual returned objective is J_N(u)=u/2 and J_N'(0)=1/2. At u=0 the stage residual is exactly zero and R_K=1/2 is nonsingular. Implicit differentiation instead gives K'(0)=2 and objective derivative 1.
counterexample.consequence: The current exact-root derivative branch can report an incorrect stationarity residual even on a locally constant stopping branch.

findings.remaining_prerequisite: The derivative must belong to the actual returned stage map. Implicit differentiation requires neighborhood agreement with the selected exact solution branch.

changes.replacement:
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice.

For every LQR data set in [[def-ctrl1-linear-lqr-control-problem]] and every admissible control $u$, an adjoint in [[def-ctrl1-lqr-adjoint-equation]] exists. If Dependent Choice is also assumed, this adjoint is unique.

[F1] The linear state lemma supplies a unique absolutely continuous solution of its integral equation for $\dot y=C(t)y+D(t)v(t)$ with $C,D\in L^\infty$ and $v\in L^2$. Under Countable Choice that constructed solution satisfies the differential equation almost everywhere ([[lem-ctrl1-measurable-linear-ode-state-map]], [[def-countable-choice]]).

[F3] Under Countable Choice and Dependent Choice, an absolutely continuous scalar function equals its initial value plus the integral of its almost-everywhere derivative; apply this componentwise ([[thm-fundamental-theorem-of-calculus-for-absolutely-continuous-functions]]).

[A1] Dependent Choice is assumed only for uniqueness ([[def-dependent-choice]]).

Apply [F1] with $D(s)=I$ and initial value $q(0)=P(x_u(T)-x_T)$ to obtain the unique absolutely continuous integral-equation solution; under Countable Choice it satisfies $\dot q=Cq+g$ almost everywhere. [F1, F2, given, construct]

3.1 For uniqueness assume [A1]. If $\widetilde p$ is another adjoint, $\widetilde q(s)=\widetilde p(T-s)$ is absolutely continuous, has the same initial value as $q$, and satisfies $\dot{\widetilde q}=C\widetilde q+g$ almost everywhere. By [F3] componentwise, $\widetilde q(s)=q(0)+\int_0^s(C(a)\widetilde q(a)+g(a))\,da$. Thus it solves the same integral equation as $q$. Uniqueness of that integral equation in [F1] gives $\widetilde q=q$, hence $\widetilde p=p$. [A1, F1, F3, step 1.1, step 2.1] ∎
